title: Docker Containers Quick Revision
summary: Quick revision notes on Docker: images vs containers, Dockerfiles and multi-stage builds, small base images, one process per container, health checks, environment configuration and local stacks with Docker Compose.

chapters.title: Images vs Containers
points: Image: read-only, layered, immutable template; container: a running (or stopped) instance of an image with a thin writable layer on top
Container is an isolated process using kernel namespaces (isolation) and cgroups (CPU/memory limits); it shares the host kernel, unlike a VM
Image vs container: image = class/recipe, container = object/instance; one image can start many containers
Example: docker run -d --name web -p 8080:80 nginx:1.27 starts a container from the nginx image, mapping host 8080 to container 80
Mistake: writing data into the container's writable layer; it is lost on docker rm, so use volumes (-v data:/var/lib/db) for state

chapters.title: Dockerfiles and Multi-Stage Builds
points: Each Dockerfile instruction (FROM, RUN, COPY) creates a layer; layers are cached and reused until an earlier layer changes
Cache-friendly order: copy dependency manifest (package.json) and install first, then COPY the source, so code edits do not reinstall dependencies
CMD = default command, overridable at docker run; ENTRYPOINT = fixed executable, CMD supplies its default args; use exec form ["node","app.js"] so signals reach the process
Multi-stage: FROM node:22 AS build ... then FROM node:22-alpine and COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist; only the final stage ships, leaving compilers and dev dependencies out
Mistake: COPY . . before installing dependencies, missing .dockerignore (node_modules, .git, .env get sent into the build context), and baking secrets into layers

chapters.title: Small Images and One Process Per Container
points: Smaller images pull faster and have a smaller attack surface; pin an explicit tag (node:22-alpine), never rely on :latest
Base image comparison: full Debian (~900MB+) vs -slim (~200MB) vs alpine (~50MB, musl libc can break native deps) vs distroless (no shell or package manager, smallest attack surface)
One process per container: each container does one job (web, worker, db), so it scales, restarts and logs independently, with logs written to stdout/stderr
Run as a non-root user: RUN adduser -D app then USER app
Mistake: running sshd or several services in one container via a supervisor, and installing debug tools and caches in the final image

chapters.title: Health Checks and Environment Configuration
points: HEALTHCHECK CMD curl -f http://localhost:3000/health || exit 1 with --interval, --timeout and --retries; status moves starting -> healthy -> unhealthy
A health check tests that the app works, not just that the process is alive: a running container can still be unhealthy, and docker ps shows the status
Twelve-factor config: the same image runs in every environment, with settings injected at runtime via docker run -e KEY=val or --env-file .env
ENV in a Dockerfile sets a default baked into the image; ARG exists only at build time; never put secrets in either (use runtime secrets)
Mistake: baking environment-specific config or secrets into the image, committing .env, and using a health check with no start period so slow apps get marked unhealthy

chapters.title: Docker Compose and Cheat Sheet
points: compose.yaml defines services (image or build, ports, environment, volumes, depends_on) that share a default network where services reach each other by service name (db:5432)
depends_on with condition: service_healthy waits for the health check, since plain depends_on only waits for the container to start
docker compose up -d --build starts the stack; docker compose down stops and removes it (-v also deletes volumes); docker compose logs -f web follows logs
Everyday commands: docker build -t app:1.0 . | docker ps -a | docker logs -f c | docker exec -it c sh | docker stop c | docker rm c | docker images | docker system prune
Quick rules: pin tags, order layers by change frequency, multi-stage for small images, non-root user, one process per container, config via env, named volumes for state
